questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14096050/assets/d2be88ec9cb7559ca8d80d528e143d4f2dd72109c9dc576b353dd352855c53ff.png)

A cube is expanding uniformly at a rate of $57{\text{ cm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ How fast is each edge of the cube increasing when the volume of the cube is $27{\text{ cm}}^{3}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side length of the cube and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=57\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ when $V=27\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the cube:

$$
V={x}^{3}
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Before we plug in the known values, we need to find the value of $x$ when $V=27\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={x}^{3} \\ 27 & ={x}^{3} \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug $x=3$ and $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=57$ into the expression for $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ 57 & =3(3)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\, \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{19}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sides of the cube are increasing at a rate of $\frac{19}{9}\,\text{cm}/\text{s}$ at the moment when $x=3\,\text{cm}.$

The length of a rectangular prism is decreasing by $3\,\text{cm}\text{/min},$ while the $5\,\text{cm}$ height does not change. If the volume of the rectangular prism is increasing at a rate of $15\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min},$  how fast is its width changing when its dimensions are $6\,\text{cm}$ in length and $2\,\text{cm}$ in width?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the solid, and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6\,\text{cm}, \\ y & =2\,\text{cm}, \\ z & =5\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-3\,\text{cm}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =15\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=6\,\text{cm},$ $y=2\,\text{cm}$ and $z=5\,\text{cm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Since $z$ is not changing and $z=5,$ we get

$$
V=5xy.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5xy) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =5x(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+5y(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =5(6)(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+5(2)(-3) \\ 15 & =30(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})-30 \\ 45 & =30(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{2}\,\text{cm}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the width of the solid is increasing at a rate of $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{cm}/\text{min}$ at the moment when $x=6\,\text{cm},$ $y=2\,\text{cm}$ and $z=5\,\text{cm}.$

A cube of ice is melting uniformly at a rate of $6\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min},$ where $x$ is the length of its edge. How fast is each edge of the ice block decreasing when the volume of the cube is $8\,{\text{cm}}^{3}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $V$ be the volume of the ice cube. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-6\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ when $V=8\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the cube:

$$
V={x}^{3}
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Before we plug in the known values, we need to find the value of $x$ when $V=8\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={x}^{3} \\ 8 & ={x}^{3} \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug $x=2$ and $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-6$ into the expression for $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ -6 & =3(2)^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sides of the cube are decreasing at a rate of $\frac{1}{2}\,\text{cm}/\text{min}$ at the moment when $x=2\,\text{cm}.$

A factory uses a rectangular mold with a fixed width of $18\,\text{in}$ and a fixed height of $10\,\text{in}.$ Liquid resin is poured in so that the resin fills the mold and the length increases as the front face moves. What is the rate of change of the length if the volume is increasing at a rate of $540\,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{min}?$

The length is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
$\text{in}/\text{min}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the rectangular prism, let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =18\,\text{in}, \\ z & =10\,\text{in}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=540\,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{min}.
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ when $y=18\,\text{in}$ and $z=10\,\text{in}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Substituting the known values, we get

$$
V=x(18)(10)=180x.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(180x) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =180(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known value into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}540 & =180(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =3\,\text{in}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length is increasing at a rate of $3\,\text{in}/\text{min}.$

$\text{ft}/\text{min}.$

Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the rectangular prism, let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6\,\text{ft}, \\ y & =4\,\text{ft}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-1.2\,{\text{ft}}^{3}/\text{min}.
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=6\,\text{ft}$ and $y=4\,\text{ft}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Substituting the known values, we get

$$
V=(6)(4)z=24z.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(24z) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =24(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known value into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1.2 & =24(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =-0.05\,\text{ft}\text{/h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water level is decreasing at a rate of $0.05\,\text{ft}/\text{min}.$

The length of the rectangular prism shown above is increasing at a rate of $7\text{ in/min}.$ What is the rate of change of the surface area of the rectangular prism?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the rectangular prism, and let $S$ be its surface area. The variables $x$ and $S$ change with time. In particular, we are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =8\text{ in}, \\ z & =12\text{ in}, \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =7\text{ in}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t}.$

We want to find the rate of change of $S$ knowing the rate of change of $x.$ So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the rectangular prism:

$$
S=2xz+2xy+2yz
$$

Substituting the known values, we get

$$
S=2(12)(x)+2x(8)+2(12)(8)=40x+192.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =40(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the above expression using $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=7,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =40(7)=280{\text{ in}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rectangular prism's surface area is increasing at a rate of $280\,{\text{in}}^{2}/\text{min}.$

The length of a rectangular prism is decreasing at a rate of $3\,\text{cm}\text{/min},$ the width is increasing at a rate of $5\,\text{cm}\text{/min},$ and the $5\,\text{cm}$ height does not change. How fast is the surface area of the rectangular prism decreasing when its dimensions are $3\,\text{cm}$ in length and $10\,\text{cm}$ in width?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the solid, and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\,\text{cm}, \\ y & =10\,\text{cm}, \\ z & =5\,\text{cm}, \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-3\,\text{cm}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =5\,\text{cm}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t}.$

We want to find the rate of change of $S$ knowing the rate of change of $x$ and $y.$ So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the rectangular prism:

$$
S=2xz+2xy+2yz
$$

Since $z=5\,\text{cm}$ is not changing, we get

$$
S=10x+2xy+10y.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10x+2xy+10y) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =(2x+10)(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+(10+2y)(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =(2\cdot 3+10)(5)+(10+2\cdot 10)(-3) \\  & =80-90 \\  & =-10\,{\text{cm}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area of the rectangular prism is decreasing at a rate of $10\,{\text{cm}}^{2}/\text{min}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side of the cube, let $S$ be its surface area, and let $V$ be its volume. All of the variables change with time. In particular, we are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-1.5\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=4\,\text{cm}.$

We want to find the rate of change of $S$ knowing the rate of change of $x.$ So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the cube:

$$
S=6{x}^{2}
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(S) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12(4)(-1.5) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =-72.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the cube's surface area is decreasing at a rate of $72\,{\text{cm}}^{2}/\text{s}.$

An elastic rectangular prism whose height is $20\text{ in}$ and width is $30\text{ in}$ is being stretched. If its length is increasing at a rate of $10\text{ in/min}$, what is the rate of change of the surface area of the rectangular prism?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the rectangular prism, let $S$ be its surface area, and let $V$ be its volume. The variables $x,S$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =20\text{ in}, \\ z & =30\text{ in}, \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =10\text{ in}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t}.$

We want to find the rate of change of $S$ knowing the rate of change of $x.$ So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the rectangular prism:

$$
S=2xz+2xy+2yz
$$

Substituting the known values, we get

$$
S=2(30)(x)+2x(20)+2(30)(20)=100x+1\,200.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =100(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the above expression using $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=10,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =100(10)=1\,000{\text{ in}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rectangular prism's surface area is increasing at a rate of $1\,000\,{\text{in}}^{2}/\text{min}.$

The edges of a cube decrease at a rate of $4\text{ cm/s}.$ At what rate is the volume decreasing when the length of each edge is $26\text{ cm}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side length of the cube and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-4\text{ cm/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=26\text{ cm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the cube:

$$
V={x}^{3}
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug $x=26$ and $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-4\text{ cm/s}$ into the expression for $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3(26)^{2}\cdot (-4)\, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-8\,112.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the cube is decreasing at a rate of $8\,112\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}$ at the moment when $x=26\,\text{cm}.$

A bar of soap wearing down with use gradually decreases in all its dimensions. Its height is decreasing at a rate of $0.05\,\text{cm/s},$ its width is decreasing at a rate of $0.1\,\text{cm/s},$ and its length is decreasing at a rate of $0.2\,\text{cm/s}.$ How fast is its volume changing when its dimensions are $12\,\text{cm}$ in length, $5\,\text{cm}$ in width, and $4\,\text{cm}$ in height? Assume that the rate of decrease of volume is positive.

The volume of the bar of soap is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $L,$ $W,$ $H$ and $V$ be the length, the width, the height, and the volume of the box, respectively. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}L=12\text{ cm},\, & W=5\text{ cm}, \\ H=4\text{ cm},\, & \frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}=-0.2\text{ cm/s}, \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{\text{d}t}=-0.1\text{ cm/s},\, & \frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}=-0.05\text{ cm/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$

The relation between the four variables is given by the formula for the volume of a rectangular prism:

$$
V=LWH
$$

We differentiate both sides of $V=LWH$ with respect to $t,$ using the product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWH) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =W\cdot H(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t})+L\cdot H(\frac{\text{d}W}{\text{d}t})+L\cdot W(\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(5)(4)(-0.2)+(12)(4)(-0.1)+(12)(5)(-0.05) \\  & =-11.8{\text{ cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the bar of soap is decreasing at a rate of $11.8{\text{ cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.$

A sugar cube is dissolving uniformly in water. If each edge of the cube decreases at a rate of $4\,\text{cm}/\text{s},$ determine the rate at which its volume is decreasing when the length of each edge is $2\,\text{cm}.$ Assume that the rate of decrease of the volume is positive.

The volume of the cube is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side length of the cube and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-4\text{ cm/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=2\text{ cm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the cube:

$$
V={x}^{3}
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug $x=2$ and $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-4\text{ cm/s}$ into the expression for $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3(2)^{2}\cdot (-4) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-48.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the cube is decreasing at a rate of $48\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}$ at the moment when $x=2\,\text{cm}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14096050/assets/acef9493a9569c023c00e67323f1ffbe8d2f424796205deafb69214838b2c4e2.png)

Water is being poured into a rectangular prism shaped tank. The length and width of this tank are $8\text{ m}$ and $4\text{ m},$ respectively. If the height of the water increases at a rate of $0.25\text{ m/hour}$, determine the rate at which the volume of stored water increases.
questions.worked_solution:
We define the following variables:

- let $L$ and $W$ be the length and width of the tank, respectively, and

- let $h$ and $V$ be the height and volume of the water in the tank, respectively.

Note that $h$ and $V$ change with time, while $L$ and $W$ are constants. 

We are given that

$$
L=8\,\text{m},\,W=4\,\text{m},\,\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{4}\,\text{m}/\text{hour}.
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$

The relation between the two time-dependent variables, $V$ and $h,$ is given by the formula for the volume of the water in the tank:

$$
V=LWh
$$

We differentiate both sides with respect to $t,$ treating both $L$ and $W$ as constants, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWh) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =LW\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(8)(4)\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =32\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water level is rising at a rate of $8\,{\text{m}}^{3}\text{/hour}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14096050/assets/6e41308fb734cdb42fe0d199a46e7db8edd25bd5d9ea5a3fabff0601a42dce51.png)

A rectangular loaf of rising bread dough is squeezed between two rigid side panels that keep its width fixed at $60\,\text{mm}.$ The length of the loaf is decreasing by $2\,\text{mm}\text{/s}$ and its height is increasing by $1\,\text{mm}\text{/s}.$ How fast is its volume changing when its dimensions are $100\,\text{mm}$ in length and $30\,\text{mm}$ in height?

The volume is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{mm}}^{3}/\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We define the following variables:

- let $L,$ $W,$ and $H$ be the length, width, and height of the bread loaf, respectively, and

- let $V$ be the volume of the bread loaf.

Note that $L,$ $H,$ and $V$ change with time, while $W$ is constant. 

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L=100\text{ mm},\, & W=60\text{ mm}, \\ H=30\text{ mm},\, & \frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}=-2\text{ mm/s}, \\ \frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}=1\text{ mm/s}\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$

The relation between the three time-dependent variables, $V,$ $H$ and $L,$ is given by the formula for the volume of bread loaf:

$$
V=LWH
$$

We differentiate both sides of $V=LWH$ with respect to $t,$ treating $W$ as a constant, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWH) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =W\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LH) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =W[L(\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t})+H(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t})] \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =W\cdot L(\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t})+W\cdot H(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(60)(100)(1)+(60)(30)(-2) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =6000-3600 \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =2400.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of bread loaf is increasing at a rate of $2400\,{\text{mm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$

canonical_examples.problem:
A cube is shrinking uniformly at a rate of $3\,\text{mm}^3/\text{s}.$ How fast is each side of the cube shrinking when the volume of the cube is $27\,\text{mm}^3?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14096050/assets/0ca7021995b1a501f6cb862b33649bdb1927f7ce4a8630a9e261382a193f40a4.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side of the cube and $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-3\,{\text{mm}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm dt}$ when $V=27\,\text{mm}^3.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the cube:

$$
V=x^3
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Before we plug in the known values, we need to find the value of $x$ when $V = 27\,\text{mm}^3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={x}^{3} \\ 27 & ={x}^{3} \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug $x=3$ and $\dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm dt}=-3$ into the expression for $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm dt}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ -3 & =3(3)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\, \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sides of the cube are shrinking at a rate of $\dfrac{1}{9}\,\text{mm}/\text{s}$ at the moment when $x=3\,\textrm{mm}.$

canonical_examples.problem:
All of the edges of a cube are increasing at a rate of $2\,\text{mm}/\text{s}.$ How fast is the surface area of the cube changing when the volume of the cube is $8\,\text{cm}^3?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14096050/assets/a6ef2af1ed8e44f82469625e232ed67c0b809a3c8199a6ce52fd2bf2e3fcffa7.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side length of the cube, let $S$ be its surface area, and let $V$ be its volume. All of the variables change with time. In particular, we are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2\,\text{mm}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\dfrac{\textrm d S}{\textrm dt}$ when $V= 8\,\text{cm}^3.$

We want to find the rate of change of $S$ knowing the rate of change of $x.$ So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the cube:

$$
S= 6x^2
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}S & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Before we plug in the known values, we need to find the value of $x$ when $V= 8\,\text{cm}^3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={x}^{3} \\ 8 & ={x}^{3} \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So $x=2\,\text{cm}=20\,\text{mm}.$

We can now plug the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12(20)(2) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =480.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the cube's surface area is changing at a rate of  $480 \,\text{mm}^2/\text{s}.$

We define the following variables:

- let $L$ and $W$ be the length and width of the tank, respectively, and

- let $h$ and $V$ be the height and volume of the water in the tank, respectively.

Note that $h$ and $V$ change with time, while $L$ and $W$ are constants. 

We are given that

$$
L=20\,\text{ft}, \qquad  W=15\,\text{ft}, \qquad  \dfrac{\textrm dh}{\textrm dt} = \dfrac{1}{6}\,\text{ft}/\text{min}.
$$

We would like to find $\dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt}.$

The relation between the two time-dependent variables, $V$ and $h,$ is given by the formula for the volume of the water in the tank:

$$
V = LWh
$$

We differentiate both sides with respect to $t,$ treating both $L$ and $W$ as constants, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWh) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =LW\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(20)(15)\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =300\cdot \frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =50.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water level is rising at a rate of $50\,\text{ft}^3\textrm{/min}.$
